text:
Your biggest risk is **a single event defeating every copy**, with permanent order loss as the worst outcome. Two application replicas share configuration and deployment failures; both database copies share an availability zone. Backups provide unproven recovery, and nightly backups alone can lose nearly a day of orders.

Assumption: an order is considered accepted only after its database transaction commits. Without failure history, we cannot establish which outage is most likely; I would prioritize irreversible loss.

1. **Prove database recovery first, and measure the data-loss window.** Restore a recent backup into an isolated environment, verify orders and application behavior, and time the recovery. Check whether continuous transaction-log archiving supports point-in-time recovery; enable it if absent and test it. Record a short recovery procedure. This establishes whether you have a usable recovery path. Point-in-time recovery still permits loss of transactions whose logs have not reached durable storage.

2. **Move the database standby to another availability zone and protect acknowledged orders.** Prefer an existing managed multi-zone database capability if available. Streaming replication does not establish zero data loss: verify whether commits wait for durable replication. If accepted orders must survive primary or zone loss, use synchronous cross-zone durability with appropriate failover fencing, accepting the latency and availability tradeoff. Test failover and verify that acknowledged orders survive.

3. **Stop deploying code and configuration to both application replicas simultaneously.** Update one replica, check health and order-processing signals, then proceed to the second; make rollback straightforward. Apply the same staging and validation to configuration. Running replicas should retain their last validated configuration during a store outage, with explicit expiry behavior for settings that cannot safely remain stale.

Start the restore exercise on day one. Use the remaining week for the smallest proven database protection and staged rollout changes your platform supports. At **$20,000 per hour**, recovery time matters—but a fast recovery that silently loses accepted orders does not meet your requirement.
